During Dia de los Muertos celebrations, women and girls in Mexico commonly dress as the famous skeletal figure known as La Catrina. In the early 1900s, artist José Guadalupe Posada created the character to satirize Mexicans who embraced European customs—a figure cloaked in European clothes, while its "bones" remain Mexican. Later popularized by artist Diego Rivera, La Catrina is the most recognizable symbol of the holiday and embodies Mexican identity.

Drag racer and auto mechanic Larry Harms has been running his autobody business in an Idaho desert since 1967. Over the years, L & L Classic Auto became one of the world’s largest salvage yards and the resting place for over 10,000 vehicles from rare Cadillacs and GMC Pacers to school buses. But in June 2026, a fast-moving wildfire swept through the yard, burning 9,000 vehicles.

"Every creature has something interesting about it, and sometimes all it takes is getting close enough to appreciate it," he tells National Geographic.

Photographer John-Oliver Dum was first drawn to jumping spiders after learning that they sometimes supplement their diet with plant-based food sources. He then set out to capture that behavior, photographing this jumping spider carrying pollen on its body. "My aim is to combine microscopy, photography, observation of animal behavior, and education," Dum says "to show that even very small and familiar creatures can reveal completely unexpected stories when we look closely enough." Dum's image won second place in the 2026 Nikon Small World Photomicrography Competition.

Forests were once found in abundance across Maryland's Eastern Shore. But due to its flat landscape, the area has been vulnerable to the effects of sea-level rise. The salinity of the soil has caused forests to massively decline, leaving behind "ghost forests" that are now ubiquitous across the Eastern Shore. Photographer Yazan Aboushi says his image captures the "haunting stalks that remain of what was once a thriving forest, now transitioning into marsh at Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge."

At Tehachapi Pass in Kern County, California, towering wind turbines cast shadows across rolling hills. Known as the birthplace of North American wind energy, Tehachapi became home to some of the continent’s first large-scale wind farms in the early 1980s. Today, generations of turbines continue to turn side by side, capturing the evolution of wind power in a landscape shaped by the wind.

Against the darkness of an early Florida morning, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket tears through the sky, creating a portrait of humanity’s reach beyond Earth. At 6:33 a.m. ET on October 13, the rocket rose from the Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Photographer Michael Seeley captured the entire spectacle in a single 426-second exposure across the Banana River, which saw the Falcon 9’s exhaust plume catching the rays of the rising sun while the landscape below remained in darkness.

White teatfish (Holothuria fuscogilva), Ras Muhammad National Park, Red Sea, Egypt. This species of sea cucumber, also known as white teeth, is found in shallow waters near islands and around coral reefs in the tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific ocean. Juvenile cucumbers live in shallower waters (such as inter-tidal zones) and then migrate to deeper waters as they mature. Adult cucumbers weigh between 2.4 and 4 kilograms. They are oval in shape and have a firm texture. This species cucumber has lateral papillae (teats) which are often buried in the sand. As it's consumed as a food and is part of a large commercial fishery across its range, it was listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List in 2010 due to overfishing.

Photographer and National Geographic Explorer Carlton Ward Jr. wanted to get close as close as possible to these Florida cracker cattle on the pastures of the state's Buck Island Ranch. Using a wide angle lens, Ward witnessed the ranchers herding the cattle on horseback before dawn. “I was looking for the layering for the story,” he tells National Geographic. “Having the cowboy near the foreground is really important, but having the other cowboys in the background on the other side of the herd kind of helps make it a more immersive experience.” Ward's exhibition, "The Wild Path: Connecting the Florida We Don’t See,” is currently on display at the Orlando Museum of Art.

View of the Basilica Cistern, Istanbul, Turkey. The Basilica Cistern, or Cisterna Basilica is the largest of several hundred ancient cisterns that lie beneath the city. This subterranean cistern was called Basilica because it was located under a large public square, the Stoa Basilica, on the First Hill of Constantinople. The cistern, built in the 6th century during the reign of Byzantine emperor Justinian I, provided a water filtration system for the Great Palace of Constantinople and other buildings on the First Hill, and continued to provide water to the Topkapı Palace after the Ottoman conquest in 1453 and into modern times. Today it is kept with little water, for public access inside the space.

When does a nebula look like a comet?  In this crowded starfield covering over two degrees within the high-flying constellation of the Swan (Cygnus), the eye is drawn to the Cocoon Nebula.  A compact star forming region, the cosmic Cocoon punctuates a nebula bright in emission and reflection on the lower right, with a long trail of interstellar dust clouds to the left, making the entire complex appear a bit like a comet.  Cataloged as IC 5146, the central bright head of the nebula spans about 10 light years, while the dark dusty tail spans nearly 100 light years.  Both are located about 2,500 light years away.  A bright star near the colorful nebula's center likely supplies power and helps clear out a cavity.  The long dusty filaments of the tail, although dark in this visible light image, hide stars in the process of formation. The featured image was captured in July from Death Valley, California, USA. This shot captured an unexpected silhouette. Which is it?  It isn't the sunspots, the small dark regions caused by concentrated magnetic fields visible around the Sun's bright disk. Sunspots typically last for weeks and were expected, since these spots were seen previously.  It isn’t the International Space Station (ISS), the small dark structure on the middle left.  This is because the featured picture was planned with sub-second timing to record the iconic structure passing before the Sun.  It is the airplane.  Just as this exposure was taking place in June, from Prasek in the Czech Republic, an airplane began its own miniature partial eclipse.  The result is this triply aligned image of our Sun.  The photographer estimates that the chance of any random Sun image containing silhouettes of both a space station and an airplane, from that location, is about 30 million to one.    APOD's main NASA site is moving: From apod.nasa.gov to science.nasa.gov/apod
